meaning: A strong, old-fashioned prohibition: “must not ...”. 「べからざる」 modifies a noun: “that must not / cannot be ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + べからず / べからざる + noun (する → するべからず / すべからず)

senses.label: Must not (prohibition)
senses.meaning: A strong ban, like “No ...!” or “Thou shalt not ...”. It sounds stiff and archaic. You see it on signs, slogans and in proverbs. In speech, people only use it jokingly.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べからず. Common: 「立ち入るべからず」, 「入るべからず」, 「忘るべからず」
examples: No entry except for authorized personnel.
Keep off the grass.
Never forget your original resolve.

senses.label: That cannot be ...
senses.meaning: 「べからざる」 + noun means “that must not / cannot be ...”. It forms set phrases like 「欠くべからざる」 (“indispensable”). Written style.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べからざる + noun. Common: 「欠くべからざる」, 「許すべからざる」, 「侵すべからざる」
examples: Water is indispensable to daily life.
That is an unforgivable act.
He is indispensable to this team.

notes: 「べからず」 is a notice-board prohibition addressed to the public at large. Said to someone's face (especially a superior or a customer), 「〜するべからず」 sounds like a stern scolding and is very rude. For spoken prohibitions use 「〜ないでください」 or 「〜はご遠慮ください」.
At the end of a sentence use 「べからず」; to modify a noun you must switch to 「べからざる」: ✕「欠くべからずもの」→ ○「欠くべからざるもの」.
It attaches only to the dictionary form of a verb, never to the ない-form or ます-form: ✕「入らないべからず」 ✕「入りますべからず」→ ○「入るべからず」.
The adverb 「すべからく」 looks similar but means something quite different: “by rights, without fail” (「学生はすべからく勉強すべし」). It is not a prohibition, and using it to mean “all” is a common mistake.

daily.title: Reading a sign
daily.description: A prohibition sign at a temple or a construction site.
daily.example: No entry beyond this point.

daily.title: Hearing a proverb
daily.description: An older person quotes an old saying to teach a young one.
daily.example: He who does not work shall not eat, you know.

daily.title: Joking around
daily.description: A note on the fridge, written in a mock-stern tone.
daily.example: This pudding: thou shalt not eat.

work.title: Company rules
work.description: A formal document listing prohibited actions.
work.example: Confidential company materials must not be taken off the premises.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: An editorial stresses how important something is.
work.example: Trust is an indispensable asset for a company.

etymology: From 「べから」, the irrealis form of the classical auxiliary 「べし」, plus the negative auxiliary 「ず」. 「ざる」 is the attributive form of 「ず」, so it can modify nouns.

similar.title: 〜てはならない
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning; both say “not allowed”. 「てはならない」 is modern written Japanese used in laws and moral lectures (「嘘をついてはならない」), while 「べからず」 is more archaic and appears almost only on signs, slogans and in proverbs.

similar.title: 〜べきではない
similar.explanation: Same origin (both come from 「べし」), but 「べきではない」 means “(by reason) should not”, which is advice or an evaluation; 「べからず」 is a prohibition that admits no discussion. Rewrite a rule as 「べきではない」 and it turns from a “ban” into a “suggestion”.

similar.title: 〜べし
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「べからず」 is simply the negation of 「べし」. 「べし」 means “must, ought to” (「早く寝るべし」) and 「べからず」 means “must not”; the two often appear side by side on the same notice.

similar.title: 〜まじき
similar.explanation: Close in meaning, as 「まじ」 can be seen as the negative counterpart of 「べし」. 「べからざる」 stresses “cannot be (lacked / forgiven)”, while 「まじき」, mostly in 「〜にあるまじき」, condemns conduct “unbecoming of one's position”.

formation: Built from the irrealis form 「べから」 of the classical auxiliary 「べし」 (“ought to”, expressing what is proper or obligatory) plus the negative auxiliary 「ず」, so literally “ought not”. 「べし」 speaks of what is right by reason or custom, so its negation is not a personal request but “not permitted by the rules”, which is why it suits signs, school rules and proverbs. The attributive form of 「ず」 is 「ざる」, so 「べからざる」 can modify a noun directly, meaning “that must not be ...”. The most common example, 「欠くべからざる」, is “not to be lacked” → “indispensable”.

meaning: Written style. Expresses purpose, “in order to ...”, with strong determination.
connection: Verb dictionary form + べく (する → するべく / すべく)

senses.label: In order to ...
senses.meaning: Someone does the second action to achieve a goal. It sounds formal and stiff. Common in news, official documents and speeches. The second clause cannot be a command or request.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べく, ... Common: 「〜を実現すべく」, 「〜を解明すべく」, 「〜になるべく」
examples: I keep working hard every day to make my dream come true.
An investigation is underway to find the cause of the accident.
He studied like crazy in order to become a doctor.

notes: The main clause cannot be a command, request or invitation: ✕「合格すべく勉強しなさい」→ ○「合格するために勉強しなさい」.
The first clause must be an action the subject can do by will, not a natural change or an involuntary result: ✕「風邪が治るべく薬を飲む」→ ○「風邪が治るように薬を飲む」.

「べく」, 「べくして」 and 「べくもない」 differ by a hair but mean quite different things: 「勝つべく練習した」 is “practiced in order to win”, 「勝つべくして勝った」 is “won, as was bound to happen”, and 「勝つべくもない」 is “has no chance of winning”.
The tone is solemn and resolute, suited to news, speeches and formal documents. Telling a friend 「旅行に行くべく貯金してる」 sounds affected; in daily talk just use 「〜ために」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report on a rescue operation.
daily.example: An all-out search continues to rescue the missing people.

daily.title: Reading a biography
daily.description: A biography describes the hero's resolve.
daily.example: He left his hometown to support his family.

work.title: Company announcement
work.description: Explaining to customers why a service changed.
work.example: We have overhauled our system in order to improve service quality.

work.title: Project report
work.description: A report explains why a team was formed.
work.example: A dedicated team was formed to open up new markets.

etymology: From 「べく」, the continuative form of the classical auxiliary 「べし」. 「べし」 expresses obligation or intention. Linked to a following clause, it came to mean “intending to ... (and so)”, that is, purpose.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: Same meaning; both express purpose. 「ために」 works in speech and writing alike, while 「べく」 is stiff written language with strong resolve, and the main clause cannot be a command or request.

similar.title: 〜んがため（に）
similar.explanation: Both are literary purpose expressions. 「んがため」 is more intense, with a flavor of “at any cost” (「勝たんがため」); 「べく」 is milder and common in news reports.

similar.title: 〜ように (purpose)
similar.explanation: 「ように」 follows non-volitional verbs, potential forms or negatives (「忘れないように」, 「聞こえるように」); 「べく」 takes only volitional actions and cannot be used this way.

similar.title: 〜べくして
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are the continuative 「べく」 of 「べし」. 「べく」 takes the “will” sense of 「べし」 and expresses purpose; 「べくして」 takes the “inevitable” sense and means “was bound to happen” (「起こるべくして起こった事故」).

formation: This is the continuative form of the classical auxiliary 「べし」. 「べし」 carries the sense of “ought to, intend to, as a matter of course”, and the continuative form exists to link a clause to what follows. So 「Xべく、Y」 becomes “(having resolved) to do X, I do Y”, i.e. “in order to X, Y”. Because its core is the strong will contained in 「べし」, the first clause must be a volitional action, and the whole sentence shows more determination than 「ために」. And since it is only a linking form, it cannot end a sentence; a main clause must always follow.

meaning: Written style. “Unbecoming of (a ...), that should never be done”, with strong condemnation.
connection: Verb dictionary form + まじき + noun (する → するまじき / すまじき); often noun + に (として) あるまじき

senses.label: Unbecoming of one's position
senses.meaning: 「〜にあるまじき」 means something does not fit a certain position or role. It is used to condemn someone's words or actions. Often with 「行為」, 「発言」, 「態度」.
senses.connection: Noun (教師, 政治家, 社会人, etc.) + に / として + あるまじき + noun
examples: Using violence against students is conduct unbecoming of a teacher.
That remark is unacceptable for a politician.

senses.label: That should never be ...
senses.meaning: Placed directly after a verb: “that must never be ...”. Very strong, stronger than 「べきではない」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + まじき + noun. Common: 「許すまじき」, 「言うまじき」
examples: That is a crime that must never be forgiven.
I said something that should never be said in front of children.

notes: It can only modify a noun and cannot end a sentence: ✕「その行為は教師にあるまじきだ」→ ○「教師にあるまじき行為だ」.

This is a very harsh condemnation, as if to say the person is “unworthy of the role”. Saying 「〜にあるまじき」 to a superior or customer is extremely rude; used about yourself (「社会人にあるまじき失態でした」) it becomes a formal, deeply sincere apology.
In modern Japanese only the combination 「あるまじき」 is really used; 「許すまじき」, 「言うまじき」 and the like are archaic. In your own writing, 「あるまじき」 or 「〜てはならない」 is safest.

daily.title: Social news
daily.description: A news report on police misconduct.
daily.example: It is a scandal unworthy of police officers, who are supposed to protect citizens.

daily.title: Chatting with a friend
daily.description: A friend talks about a celebrity's gaffe.
daily.example: That's no way for an adult to behave, right?

work.title: Disciplinary notice
work.description: HR explains the penalty for an employee who broke the rules.
work.example: This incident was conduct unbecoming of an employee and will be dealt with strictly.

work.title: Newspaper editorial
work.description: Commenting on an official's wrongdoing.
work.example: Misconduct unworthy of a civil servant has come to light.

etymology: 「まじき」 is the attributive form of the classical negative conjectural auxiliary 「まじ」. 「まじ」 is the negative counterpart of 「べし」, meaning “should not, will not”.

similar.title: 〜べからず／〜べからざる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning, since 「まじ」 and 「べし」 are a negative/positive pair. 「べからざる」 stresses “must not be (lacked / forgiven)” and is usually an objective judgment; 「まじき」 stresses “unbecoming of one's status” and carries strong blame.

similar.title: 〜べきではない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both say “should not”. 「べきではない」 is everyday modern advice and can end a sentence; 「まじき」 is archaic, only modifies nouns, and condemns far more sharply.

similar.title: 〜まい
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「まい」 is generally thought to have developed from 「まじ」. 「まい」 can end a sentence and expresses negative will or conjecture (「二度と行くまい」); 「まじき」 only modifies nouns and means “that should not be”.

formation: This is the attributive form of 「まじ」, the classical negative-conjecture auxiliary. 「まじ」 can be seen as the negation of 「べし」, meaning “by reason absolutely ought not”. The most common pattern is the verb 「ある」 (“to exist”) + 「まじき」 = “that ought not to exist”, preceded by 「noun + に／として」 to name the standing: 「教師にあるまじき行為」 is “conduct that should never be found in a teacher”. Something that “should not exist given the status” has appeared, so it naturally carries a tone of blame: “unbecoming, intolerable”. Being an attributive form, it can only modify nouns and cannot end a sentence.

meaning: Shows resolve, “if worst comes to worst, I'll just ...”, or explains oneself, “I merely ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form + までだ / までのことだ

senses.label: I'll just ... then
senses.meaning: If the first option fails, you will simply do this instead, and that's no big deal. It shows a “so what” determination. Often paired with 「〜なら」, 「〜ても」, 「〜ば」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + までだ / までのことだ. Common: 「〜ならば、〜までだ」
examples: If there are no trains, I'll just walk home.
If I fail, I'll simply start over.
If it really doesn't work, I'll just give up.

senses.label: I merely ...
senses.meaning: You only did something, with no other intention. Used to explain or justify yourself in a low-key way.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + までだ / までのことだ. Common: 「〜たまでだ」, 「〜たまでのことです」
examples: I was only telling the truth.
I was just asking, that's all.
I was merely following the rules.

notes: The dictionary form and the た-form mean completely different things: 「歩いて帰るまでだ」 is “at worst I'll just walk home” (resolve, a fallback), whereas 「歩いて帰ったまでだ」 is “all I did was walk home” (a defense).

The た-form 「〜たまでです」 is a way of downplaying and defending yourself. Said to a boss who is pressing you, 「指示に従ったまでです」 sounds like shifting blame or talking back, so use it with care; 「ご指示どおりに対応いたしました」 is safer.
It follows verbs only, not nouns or adjectives directly: ✕「冗談までだ」→ ○「冗談で言ったまでだ」.

daily.title: Asked about your plans
daily.description: A friend worries you won't get a ticket.
daily.example: If I can't get a ticket, I'll just watch the stream at home.

daily.title: When misunderstood
daily.description: Someone thinks you were being sarcastic, so you explain.
daily.example: I wasn't being sarcastic. I just said what I thought.

daily.title: Talking about exams
daily.description: Showing you aren't afraid of failing.
daily.example: If I fail this year, I'll simply take it again next year.

work.title: Negotiating with a client
work.description: Stating your position when the other side rejects your terms.
work.example: If the terms don't work, we'll simply look for another business partner.

work.title: Praised by your boss
work.description: Replying modestly.
work.example: Not at all. I only did what a manager should do.

etymology: The particle 「まで」 marks the end point or limit of a range. “Up to this point and no further” came to mean “that's all there is to it” or “going this far is enough”.

similar.title: 〜ばそれまでだ
similar.explanation: Same core: both rest on 「まで」 for “the end point”. 「〜ばそれまでだ」 means “once ..., it's all over” (「死んでしまえばそれまでだ」), not “at worst I'll just ...”, and the two are often confused.

similar.title: 〜にすぎない
similar.explanation: Close to the た-form 「〜たまでだ」; both mean “nothing more than”. 「にすぎない」 takes nouns and quantities (「噂にすぎない」) and is an objective assessment; 「たまでだ」 takes only your own actions and sounds defensive.

similar.title: 〜ほかない・〜よりほかない
similar.explanation: Close to the dictionary-form 「〜までだ」; both mean “there is no choice but to”. 「ほかない」 is resigned acceptance; 「までだ」 treats it as a fallback, in a crisper tone with a “so what?” resolve.

similar.title: 〜までもない・〜までもなく
similar.explanation: Same origin, using 「まで」 for “going that far”. 「までもない」 means “no need to go that far” (「言うまでもない」); 「までだ」 means “going that far is enough”.

formation: Built from the limit particle 「まで」 (the end point of a range) plus the copula 「だ」 (or the nominalizers 「の」「こと」 + 「だ」), literally “it goes only as far as X”. After the dictionary form, X is something that has not happened yet: “things will go at most as far as X” → X is treated as the last resort → “at worst, I'll just do X”. After the た-form, X is something already done: “what I did went no further than X” → “I merely did X”, which gives it a defensive, downplaying tone. Adding 「のこと」 nominalizes the matter and stresses “that's all it amounts to”.

meaning: Covered with dirt or liquid on the surface; figuratively, mired in something bad.
connection: Noun + まみれ (だ / の + noun / になる)

senses.label: Covered in (literal)
senses.meaning: The whole body or a surface is covered in mud, blood, sweat, dust, etc. Usually something unpleasant, giving a sense of being a mess.
senses.connection: Noun (泥, 汗, 血, ほこり, 油, etc.) + まみれ. Common: 「泥まみれになる」, 「汗まみれの〜」
examples: The children were playing and got covered in mud.
I washed my sweat-soaked shirt.
A dust-covered book turned up in the storeroom.

senses.label: Mired in (figurative)
senses.meaning: Someone or something is full of negative things, such as debt, scandal or lies.
senses.connection: Noun (借金, 疑惑, 嘘, etc.) + まみれ
examples: He is living a life buried in debt.
That politician is riddled with suspicion.

notes: 「まみれ」 is used only for liquid or powdery stuff coating a surface (mud, sweat, blood, oil, dust). For things that are “everywhere, in great number” use 「だらけ」: ✕「傷まみれ」「間違いまみれ」→ ○「傷だらけ」「間違いだらけ」.
It is used almost only for negative things; with good things it sounds odd or ironic: ✕「幸せまみれ」→ ○「幸せいっぱい」.
「借金まみれ」 and 「疑惑まみれ」 are strongly derogatory, and very rude when said about the listener or their company.
The verb 「まみれる」 takes 「に」 for the thing covering: ○「血にまみれた手」「汗にまみれて働く」.

daily.title: Kids come home from playing
daily.description: A mother sees the state of her child.
daily.example: What happened? You're covered in mud!

daily.title: After exercise
daily.description: Complaining to a friend after a run.
daily.example: By the time I finished running, I was drenched in sweat.

daily.title: Spring cleaning
daily.description: Cleaning a room that hasn't been used in ages.
daily.example: The air-conditioner filter was caked with dust.

work.title: Factory work
work.description: Describing mechanics' working conditions.
work.example: The mechanics are working covered in grease.

work.title: Business news
work.description: A report on a company's worsening finances.
work.example: That company is drowning in debt and on the verge of bankruptcy.

etymology: From the continuative form of the verb 「まみれる（塗れる）」, “to be smeared with, to be covered in”. Usually written in kana.

similar.title: 〜だらけ
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning; both are mostly negative. 「だらけ」 means things are everywhere or excessive in number (傷, 間違い, ゴミ); 「まみれ」 stresses a liquid or powder sticking to the surface and dirtying the whole (泥, 汗, 血). Both 「泥だらけ」 and 「泥まみれ」 are possible, the latter feeling more “smeared all over”.

similar.title: 〜ずくめ
similar.explanation: Also means “all ...”, but 「ずくめ」 is mostly used for good or neutral things (「いいことずくめ」, 「黒ずくめ」) and stresses uniformity; 「まみれ」 means covered with something dirty and is almost always negative.

formation: This is the continuative form 「まみれ」 of the verb 「まみれる」 (“to be covered all over with (liquid, powder, etc.), to be soiled”), used as a noun. Noun X + 「まみれ」 = “the state of being covered with X”, and it can take 「だ」, 「の」 or 「になる」. Because the original meaning is “getting smeared and dirty”, the noun must be something that can cling to a surface, and it naturally has a negative color. Figurative uses like 「借金まみれ」 and 「疑惑まみれ」 also treat abstract bad things as “filth smeared all over that won't wash off”.

meaning: Follows a noun: “to have a touch of ..., to seem somewhat like ...”.
connection: Noun + めく / めいて / めいた + noun

senses.label: A touch of ...
senses.meaning: Usually with seasons: the feel of that season is gradually arriving. Often with 「〜てきた」. It sounds elegant and lyrical.
senses.connection: 春, 秋, 夏, etc. + めく. Common: 「春めいてきた」, 「秋めいた風」
examples: The sunlight has become quite spring-like.
Mornings and evenings feel quite autumnal now, don't they?

senses.label: Sort of like ...
senses.meaning: Not exactly the thing, but with that flavor or appearance. Usually 「〜めいた + noun」. Often slightly negative or subtle.
senses.connection: Noun (皮肉, 謎, 冗談, 言い訳, 説教, etc.) + めいた + noun / めいて
examples: He spoke in a somewhat sarcastic tone.
She gave a mysterious smile.
I don't want to say anything that sounds like an excuse.

senses.label: Pretending to be ...
senses.meaning: The transitive form 「〜めかす」 means to deliberately give that appearance. The most common is 「冗談めかして」, “half-jokingly”.
senses.connection: Noun + めかす / めかして. Common: 「冗談めかして」
examples: He half-jokingly said what he really thought.

notes: 「めく」 is a verb, so you cannot add 「な」 as with an adjective: ✕「謎めいな人」→ ○「謎めいた人」. Use 「めいた」 to modify nouns and mostly 「めいてきた」 as a predicate.
Only a limited set of nouns works (春・秋・冗談・皮肉・謎・言い訳・説教・脅し, etc.); do not coin new ones freely. For a general “-like” use 「〜っぽい」 or 「〜みたいな」.

「めいて」 means “naturally having a hint of ...”, while 「めかして」 means “deliberately pretending to be ...”: 「冗談めいた話」 is “a remark that sounds like a joke”, 「冗談めかして言う」 is “say it as if joking (while actually serious)”.
「説教めいた」, 「言い訳めいた」 and 「皮肉めいた」 are all derogatory; saying 「部長のお話は説教めいていますね」 to your boss is very rude.

daily.title: Seasonal greetings
daily.description: Chatting about the weather with a neighbor.
daily.example: It's really starting to feel like spring, isn't it?

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a mysterious character.
daily.example: The man left a cryptic remark and went away.

daily.title: Chatting with friends
daily.description: Talking about something a friend said as a joke.
daily.example: He said it half-jokingly, but I think he meant it.

work.title: Seasonal letter
work.description: The seasonal greeting at the start of a business letter.
work.example: Autumn is deepening day by day. We hope this finds you well.

work.title: Meeting feedback
work.description: Describing a boss's talk that felt like a lecture.
work.example: The department manager's preachy talk went on for a full thirty minutes.

etymology: 「めく」 is an old suffix that attaches to nouns and other words to form verbs meaning “to show signs of ...”. Words like 「ときめく」 and 「きらめく」 also come from it.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both say “a bit like ...”. 「っぽい」 is colloquial and goes with almost any noun (「子どもっぽい」, 「水っぽい」); 「めく」 is literary and takes only a fixed few nouns, mostly for seasonal feel or manner of speaking.

similar.title: 〜じみる
similar.explanation: Close; both are verb-forming suffixes meaning “take on the look of ...”. 「じみる」 usually carries a negative judgment (「年寄りじみた」, 「所帯じみた」); 「めく」 is more neutral, and 「春めく」 or 「謎めく」 can even sound elegant.

similar.title: 〜らしい (typical, befitting)
similar.explanation: 「らしい」 means “fully has the characteristics X should have” (「春らしい天気」 = typical spring weather); 「めく」 only means “starting to take on a touch of X” (「春めいてきた」 = it's getting spring-like).

similar.title: 〜ぶる
similar.explanation: Close to 「めかす」; both can mean “deliberately pretend”. 「ぶる」 is putting on airs (「偉ぶる」, 「いい子ぶる」) and is clearly derogatory; 「めかす」 is mostly using a certain tone to cover the real intent (「冗談めかす」).

formation: 「めく」 is an old suffix that attaches to nouns (and some adverbs and mimetic words) to form a godan verb meaning “to show the look of X, to take on a touch of X”. Being a verb, it appears as 「めいてきた」 (gradually taking on) or 「めいた」 (already has it, modifying a noun). It speaks only of appearance and atmosphere, not of really being X: 「春めく」 is “to feel like spring”, not “spring has arrived”, and 「皮肉めいた」 is “sounding sarcastic”. Its transitive counterpart 「めかす」 means “deliberately make it seem like X”, which gives 「冗談めかして」.

meaning: “... goes without saying, but (even more) ...”. It acknowledges the first item and puts more weight on the second.
connection: Noun + もさることながら

senses.label: Not only ... but also
senses.meaning: First grants that the first item is obviously important or excellent, then brings up a second point that deserves even more attention. Formal. The two items are usually different aspects of the same thing.
senses.connection: Noun + もさることながら、noun + も / こそ / が ... Common: 「味もさることながら」, 「〜もさることながら、〜も大切だ」
examples: The food at this restaurant is great, of course, but the service is wonderful too.
Her singing goes without saying, and her acting is also highly praised.
Exam results matter, but the effort that leads to them matters even more.

notes: The first item is “good and important, of course”, and the second is what you really want to stress; swap them and the emphasis flips: 「味もさることながら、サービスもいい」 puts the weight on service.
The two items must be judged in the same direction (both good or both important); it cannot express contrast: ✕「味もさることながら、サービスは悪い」→ ○「味はいいが、サービスは悪い」.
「も」 cannot be dropped or replaced with 「は」: ✕「味はさることながら」→ ○「味もさることながら」.

daily.title: Recommending a place
daily.description: Telling a friend about an inn.
daily.example: The food at that inn is great, of course, but the view is the best part.

daily.title: After a movie
daily.description: Sharing impressions with a friend.
daily.example: The story was good, but the music was amazing.

work.title: Product presentation
work.description: A salesperson introduces a new product to a client.
work.example: This product excels not only in performance but also in design.

work.title: Performance review
work.description: Evaluating an employee's abilities.
work.example: His expertise goes without saying, but it's his character that earns people's trust.

etymology: 「さる」 is the attributive form of classical 「然り（さり）」, “to be so, to be natural”. 「ながら」 marks contrast. Literally: “that is true enough, but ...”.

similar.title: 〜はもとより・〜はもちろん
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both say “A goes without saying, and B too ...”. 「はもとより」 extends the range from A to B with A and B on equal footing; 「もさることながら」 stresses that B deserves even more attention.

similar.title: 〜は言うまでもなく
similar.explanation: Close; 「は言うまでもなく」 says “A needs no mention” directly, while 「もさることながら」 first acknowledges A's worth and then shifts the weight to B, which is softer and more like a critic's voice.

similar.title: 〜はおろか
similar.explanation: Similar in form (A ..., B too ...), but 「はおろか」 is mostly used for negative, surprising cases (「漢字はおろか、ひらがなも書けない」); 「もさることながら」 is for positive evaluation, so they cannot be swapped.

similar.title: 〜のみならず
similar.explanation: Both mean “not only A but also B”. 「のみならず」 is a plain extension of range and can follow verbs and adjectives; 「もさることながら」 follows only nouns and stresses B more.

formation: Built from 「も」 + 「さる」 + 「こと」 + 「ながら」. 「さる」 is the attributive form of the classical 「さり」 (“to be so”), meaning “such, as is only natural”; 「ながら」 here marks concession, “although”. Literally: “A too is only natural, but ...”. You first grant that A is already good and needs no comment, then use the concessive to turn the topic to B, so B is the point. Since the first part is “A too”, the second is usually “B too / B even more”, both judged in the same direction.

meaning: “If only ..., but ...”. Expresses regret, dissatisfaction or reproach.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + ものを (often paired with 「〜ば」 or 「〜たら」)

senses.label: If only ...
senses.meaning: At the end or in the middle of a sentence: things could have turned out better, but they didn't. It shows regret. Often 「〜ば〜たものを」.
senses.connection: 〜ば / 〜たら + verb ta-form + ものを. Common: 「〜ばよかったものを」
examples: If you'd told me sooner, I would have helped.
If only I'd been a little more careful.
If you had apologized honestly, I would have forgiven you.

senses.label: Even though ...
senses.meaning: A contrast, like 「のに」. The other person didn't do what they should have, with reproach or dissatisfaction. The second clause is usually a bad result.
senses.connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + ものを、... Common: 「〜ばいいものを」
examples: You could have just kept quiet, but you said something unnecessary, and that's why you got scolded.
He should have left it alone, but he meddled again.

notes: 「ものを」 means “you could have ..., but didn't”, and is used only for chances already missed and irreversible; the following clause is often omitted, and the sentence-final 「ものを」 itself carries regret or reproach.
It has a clear tone of blame. Saying 「言ってくだされば手伝ったものを」 to a boss or customer sounds like a complaint; the polite versions are 「お声がけいただければ、お手伝いいたしましたのに」 or 「次回はぜひお声がけください」.
The 「ものを」 in 「新しいものを買う」 is just “thing + を” and not this grammar; this grammar appears mostly at the end of a sentence or before a comma, often after 「〜ば（たら）…た」 or 「〜ばいい」.

daily.title: A friend gets hurt
daily.description: A friend pushed too hard and got injured, and you feel sorry.
daily.example: If only you hadn't overdone it.

daily.title: Family argument
daily.description: Blaming a family member for butting in.
daily.example: You could have just left it alone. Why did you have to interfere?

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character laments a missed chance.
daily.example: If I had just said sorry back then, we wouldn't have broken up.

work.title: A mistake at work
work.description: A coworker didn't report a problem in time, and it got worse.
work.example: If you had reported it right away, we could have dealt with it.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: Criticizing a company's slow response.
work.example: The damage could have been prevented with early measures, but the response came too late.

etymology: Formed from the formal noun 「もの」 + the particle 「を」. In classical Japanese, 「ものを」 was already a conjunctive particle of contrast (“although”) and a sentence-final particle of regret or exclamation.

similar.title: 〜のに（逆接）
similar.explanation: The closest; sentence-final 「のに」 and 「ものを」 both express regret or dissatisfaction. 「のに」 is used in speech and writing and can also express plain surprise; 「ものを」 is more literary and emotional, focusing on “could have ...”.

similar.title: 〜だろうに
similar.explanation: Close; both express regret that “it should have been ... but ...”. 「だろうに」 includes conjecture and is often sympathetic (「疲れているだろうに」); 「ものを」 mostly regrets or blames something left undone.

similar.title: 〜ばよかった
similar.explanation: Close; both mean “if only ...”. 「ばよかった」 states regret directly and is mostly about yourself; 「〜ば…たものを」 spells out “the result that could have been” and is more often used to blame others.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: Same origin; both are built on the formal noun 「もの」 and both are concessive. 「ものの」 just says objectively “although ..., ...” (「買ったものの、使っていない」), with no regret or blame.

formation: Built from the formal noun 「もの」 plus the particle 「を」. In classical Japanese 「を」 could serve not only as an object marker but also as a conjunctive particle of contrast, so 「ものを」 as a whole means “even though it is so, ...”. In modern use it pairs with 「〜ば（たら）…た」: the first half supposes “if you had done so”, 「…たものを」 states “the result that could have been”, and the contrastive 「を」 sets it against reality: “it would have been fine if ..., but ...”. The following clause is often dropped, leaving the sentence-final 「ものを」 with just a lingering note of regret or reproach.

meaning: Written style. “As soon as ...”: the second event happens right after the first.
connection: Verb dictionary form + や否や / やいなや / や

senses.label: As soon as ...
senses.meaning: Something happens almost at the same moment the first action occurs. The second event is often sudden or unexpected. Describes past facts, so the second clause is usually in the ta-form.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + や否や (やいなや)、... た
examples: The moment the bell rang, the students rushed out of the classroom.
As soon as he got home, he collapsed onto the bed.
The new product sold out as soon as it was released.

senses.label: Short form 「や」
senses.meaning: Drops 「否や」 and uses just 「や」, with the same meaning. Even more literary, usually followed by a comma.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + や、... た
examples: The moment the door opened, a child came running in.
The moment she saw my face, she burst into tears.

notes: The main clause cannot express the speaker's will, a command or a request: ✕「家に着くや否や電話してください」→ ○「家に着いたらすぐ電話してください」／「着き次第お電話ください」.
It attaches only to the dictionary form, not the た-form: ✕「ベルが鳴ったや否や」→ ○「ベルが鳴るや否や」.
It differs from 「か否か」 by one character but means something entirely different: 「や否や」 is “as soon as ...”, 「か否か」 is “whether or not” (「参加するか否か」 = whether to participate or not).
The short form 「や」 is normally followed by a comma; do not confuse it with the 「AやB」 of listing: 「ドアが開くや、子どもが駆け込んできた」.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's hurried action.
daily.example: As soon as she read the letter, she ran out of the house.

daily.title: Sports news
daily.description: A report on how a match opened.
daily.example: No sooner had the match begun than the other team scored first.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a rush for tickets.
work.example: The tickets sold out the moment sales began.

work.title: Market analysis
work.description: Describing how fast the market reacted.
work.example: As soon as the tax hike was announced, consumers started stockpiling.

etymology: 「や」 is a classical question particle, and 「否（いな）」 means “no”. 「〜や否や」 is thought to have originally meant “before it is clear whether ... or not”: the next thing happens before you can tell if the first is finished. Hence “as soon as”.

similar.title: 〜が早いか
similar.explanation: The closest; both mean “no sooner ... than ...”, and neither allows will or commands in the second clause. 「が早いか」 stresses the speed of the action, almost anticipating it; 「や否や」 describes the instant scene and is more literary.

similar.title: 〜なり (as soon as)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「なり」 requires the same subject in both clauses and usually a surprising act in the second (「顔を見るなり泣き出した」); 「や否や」 allows different subjects.

similar.title: 〜か〜ないかのうちに
similar.explanation: Close, but 「か〜ないかのうちに」 stresses that the second event begins before the first has quite finished; 「や否や」 means the second follows right on the heels of the first. The former is also usable in speech.

similar.title: 〜たとたん（に）
similar.explanation: Close; 「たとたん」 follows the た-form, is common in speech, and the second clause is usually unexpected; 「や否や」 follows the dictionary form, is literary, and reports past facts.

formation: Built from the classical interrogative particle 「や」 + 「否」 (“no, not”) + 「や」. The original sense is thought to be “is it done, or not?”, i.e. before one could even judge whether the first action was complete. Applied to two events: while the first is still in that moment of “done yet? not yet?”, the second has already happened → “as soon as ..., ...”. Because it describes observed fact, the second clause is an objective occurrence and cannot take a command or will; dropping 「否や」 and keeping only 「や」 expresses the same instant.

meaning: Written style. Expresses cause, “because of ...”. At the start of a sentence, 「ゆえに」 means “therefore”.
connection: Noun (の) / na-adjective (である) / plain form + ゆえ（に）/ ゆえの + noun; often 「〜がゆえに」

senses.label: Because of ...
senses.meaning: Gives a cause or reason. Stiff and formal, found in writing and speeches. 「〜がゆえに」 is stronger.
senses.connection: Noun + ゆえ（に）; plain form / noun + である + がゆえに
examples: Because of poverty, he couldn't go to school.
Precisely because he is honest, he often loses out.
Given the circumstances, we ask for your understanding.

senses.label: ... that comes from ...
senses.meaning: 「ゆえの + noun」 means “... that arises because of ...”. A typical phrase is 「若さゆえの過ち」.
senses.connection: Noun + ゆえの + noun; 〜がゆえの + noun
examples: That was a mistake of youth.
There are worries that come precisely from being a parent.

senses.label: Therefore (sentence-initial)
senses.meaning: At the start of a sentence, it works as a conjunction like 「だから」 or 「したがって」. Used in logical reasoning such as math proofs and academic papers.
senses.connection: Start of sentence + ゆえに (故に)、...
examples: A equals B, and B equals C. Therefore, A equals C.
I think, therefore I am.

notes: The style is stiff: in everyday talk or ordinary emails 「〜ゆえに」 sounds old-fashioned and affected, so use 「から」 or 「ので」; but set phrases like 「若さゆえの過ち」 and 「〜であるがゆえに」 are natural in writing.
To modify a noun use 「ゆえの」: ✕「若さゆえに過ち」→ ○「若さゆえの過ち」. After verbs and adjectives 「が」 is usually added: 「正直であるがゆえに」「知っているがゆえに」.
Sentence-initial 「ゆえに」 is a logical “therefore”, used in argument and proof, not to tell everyday cause and effect: ✕「雨が降った。ゆえに家にいた。」→ ○「雨が降ったから、家にいた。」
The kanji 「故」 is read 「こ」 in 「事故」, 「故障」 and 「故郷」, which is unrelated to this grammar; in this grammar it is read 「ゆえ」.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character looks back on the past.
daily.example: With the recklessness of youth, I ran away from home without thinking.

daily.title: Watching a documentary
daily.description: The narrator explains how an animal survives.
daily.example: Precisely because they are small, they protect themselves in groups.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: Drawing a conclusion in an argument.
work.example: The experimental results above support the hypothesis. Therefore, the aim of this study can be said to have been achieved.

work.title: Formal greeting
work.description: Explaining a reason in a formal message.
work.example: As I am still new to this, I may cause you some inconvenience, but I look forward to working with you.

etymology: 「ゆえ」 is written 「故」 and originally means “reason, cause”. Classical Japanese often used 「〜ゆえに」 for causes, and it survives today in written language.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: Same meaning; both express cause. 「から」 is everyday language and can be followed by requests or commands; 「ゆえ（に）」 is literary, used in argument and commentary, and the second clause is generally an objective result.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: The causal use of 「ために」 (「事故のために遅れた」) is close to 「ゆえに」, and both lean literary. 「ゆえに」 is more archaic and has fixed forms such as 「〜がゆえに」 and 「ゆえの」.

similar.title: 〜ばかりに
similar.explanation: Both express cause, but 「ばかりに」 stresses “just because of this one thing” leading to a bad result, with regret; 「ゆえに」 states cause and effect objectively, and the result can be good or bad.

similar.title: 〜からこそ
similar.explanation: 「〜がゆえに」 often carries the emphasis of “precisely because ...”, close to 「からこそ」. 「からこそ」 is used in speech and writing; 「がゆえに」 is solemn written language.

formation: The core is the noun 「ゆえ（故）」, originally “reason, cause”. 「Aゆえに」 = “A as the reason + the causal 「に」” → “because of A”; 「Aゆえの＋noun」 = “... that comes from A”. The 「が」 in 「〜がゆえに」 is an old attributive particle equivalent to 「の」, so 「AがゆえにB」 is literally “B for A's sake”, preserving classical grammar and hence its solemn tone. At the start of a sentence it takes the whole preceding text as the “reason”: “for the above reason” → “therefore”, which is how it became a connective of logical inference.

meaning: “Apart from ..., there is no (other) ...”. Praises someone or something as the only suitable choice.
connection: Noun + をおいて (ほかに) ... ない

senses.label: No one / nothing but ...
senses.meaning: There is no other suitable person or thing. It expresses high praise. Always paired with a negative.
senses.connection: Noun + をおいて (ほかに / 他に) ... ない / いない
examples: He is the only one we can entrust with this job.
If you want to learn traditional Japanese culture, there's no place like Kyoto.
Ms. Tanaka is probably the only person fit to be the next president.

senses.label: Above all else
senses.meaning: The set phrase 「何をおいても」 means “putting everything else aside, first ...”. It stresses priority.
senses.connection: 何をおいても + expression of will or obligation
examples: When an earthquake hits, you should first and foremost make sure you are safe.
When I heard my mother had collapsed, I dropped everything and rushed to her.

notes: It must be matched with a negative such as 「ほかに〜ない」; drop the negation and the meaning changes completely: 「彼をおいて出かけた」 is “went out leaving him behind”, whereas 「彼をおいてほかにいない」 is “there is no one but him”.
It is used only to praise “the one suitable person or thing”, never for negatives: ✕「彼をおいて悪い人はいない」.
「何をおいても」 means “whatever else, first of all ...”, which differs from 「Aをおいてほかにない」; do not mix them up.
It is usually written in kana 「おいて」; in kanji it should be 「措いて」, and writing 「置いて」 invites the reading “put down”.

daily.title: Recommending a place
daily.description: Telling a friend where to see cherry blossoms.
daily.example: For cherry blossoms, nothing beats Yoshino.

daily.title: A friend needs help
daily.description: A friend is in trouble, and you decide to help first.
daily.example: If a friend is in trouble, I'll drop everything and go help.

work.title: Proposing a leader
work.description: Recommending a project leader at a meeting.
work.example: I can't think of anyone but Mr. Yamamoto to lead this project.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: Commenting on an athlete's ability.
work.example: He is probably the one and only favorite to win this tournament.

etymology: The verb 「おく（置く）」 can mean “to set aside, to exclude”. 「〜をおいて」 literally means “if you set ... aside (there is nothing else)”.

similar.title: 〜を除いて
similar.explanation: Both can be translated “except for ...”. 「を除いて」 is a plain objective exclusion (「日曜を除いて営業」); 「をおいて」 is followed by a negative and aims to stress “only A will do”, with high praise.

similar.title: 〜に限る
similar.explanation: Close; both mean “A is the best”. 「に限る」 is the speaker's subjective recommendation (「夏はビールに限る」); 「をおいてほかにない」 is more formal and stresses “there is no other choice”.

similar.title: 〜にほかならない
similar.explanation: Both stress “precisely A, nothing else”. 「にほかならない」 asserts a cause or essence (「努力の結果にほかならない」); 「をおいて」 evaluates the only suitable person or place.

formation: Built from 「を」 + the te-form of the verb 「おく（措く）」. Here 「おく」 does not mean “place” but “set aside, leave out, except”. 「Aをおいて」 is “setting A aside”, and with 「ほかに〜ない」 the whole sentence says “apart from A, nowhere else can be found” → A is the only one. Contrasting A with “nothing without A” itself elevates A, so it is used only for positive evaluation. 「何をおいても」 is “whatever you set aside” → “at all costs, first of all”.

meaning: Marks a point in time as the last; after it, something stops. Also used in 「声を限りに」, “at the top of one's voice”.
connection: Noun (今日, 本日, 今回, etc.) + を限りに

senses.label: As of ... (last time)
senses.meaning: Something that has been going on ends at this point in time. Used to announce quitting, retiring or closing. The second clause is usually about ending or stopping.
senses.connection: Time noun (今日, 本日, 今回, 今年度, etc.) + を限りに
examples: As of today, I'm quitting smoking.
Our store will close its doors after today.
She will retire at the end of this season.

senses.label: With all one's might
senses.meaning: The set phrase 「声を限りに」 means shouting as loudly as possible. It is a fixed expression.
senses.connection: 声 + を限りに + 叫ぶ, 呼ぶ, etc.
examples: He cried for help at the top of his voice.
The spectators cheered the players at the top of their lungs.

notes: It differs completely from 「に限り」: 「本日を限りに閉店」 is “today is the last day, closed from now on”, while 「本日に限り半額」 is “half price today only”.
The second clause is “it ends here, no more from now on” (やめる・引退・閉店), and cannot be used for starting something new: ✕「今日を限りに新しい仕事を始める」→ ○「今日を機に／今日から新しい仕事を始める」.
It usually follows time nouns meaning “now, this time” (今日・本日・今回・今シーズン); for past events use 「〜を最後に」: 「昨年の大会を最後に引退した」.
「声を限りに」 means “shouting at the top of one's voice, with all one's might”, not “the voice ends here”.

daily.title: Making a resolution
daily.description: Telling your family you'll break a bad habit.
daily.example: Starting today, no more staying up late!

daily.title: Sports news
daily.description: A report that a famous athlete is retiring.
daily.example: I heard that player is retiring after this tournament.

work.title: Closing notice
work.description: A notice posted by a shop that is closing.
work.example: We regret to inform you that we will cease business as of today.

work.title: Farewell speech
work.description: Saying goodbye to coworkers at a farewell party.
work.example: I will be leaving the company at the end of this month. Thank you for everything.

etymology: 「限り」 is the noun form of the verb 「限る」, meaning “limit, boundary”. 「〜を限りに」 means “taking ... as the limit”, hence “with ... as the last”.

similar.title: 〜をもって
similar.explanation: Close in the deadline sense: 「本日をもって閉店」 ≈ 「本日を限りに閉店」. 「をもって」 is official notice language that just marks the point in time; 「を限りに」 stresses the resolve or farewell of “never again after this”.

similar.title: 〜を境に
similar.explanation: Both take a point in time as the boundary. 「を境に」 stresses that the situation changes before and after (「あの日を境に人が変わった」); 「を限りに」 stresses that something ends there.

similar.title: 〜に限り
similar.explanation: Same origin (both from 「限る」). 「に限り」 is the restriction “only for ...” (「先着百名に限り」); 「を限りに」 is “with ... as the last”, so the two mean entirely different things.

similar.title: 〜限り
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「限り」 has the sense “as far as possible, to the utmost” (「できる限り」, 「力の限り」), which parallels the “with all one's might” of 「声を限りに」; both come from the idea of “limit”.

formation: 「限り」 is the noun form of the verb 「限る」 (“to draw a limit”), meaning “limit, end”. 「Aを限りに」 = “taking A as the limit”: A is the last moment, and after A it does not continue, so it means “with A as the cutoff, never ... again”. The “limit” can also be the limit of one's capacity: 「声を限りに」 = “using the voice to its limit” → “shouting with all one's might”. Both senses come from the single core of 「限り」: “end point, limit”.

meaning: Starting with one event, similar events follow one after another.
connection: Noun + を皮切りに (して) / を皮切りとして

senses.label: Starting with ...
senses.meaning: Something is the first of a series of actions or events. The second clause usually means “one after another, in succession, spreading”. Common with events, tours and business expansion.
senses.connection: Noun + を皮切りに (して)、... (次々と, 相次いで, 全国で, etc.); noun + を皮切りとして
examples: Kicking off with the Tokyo show, the nationwide tour is about to begin.
Starting with his comment, objections came one after another.
Starting with this store, we plan to open ten stores overseas.

notes: The second clause must be a series of similar events unfolding one after another; it cannot be used when only one thing happens or it is merely one change: ✕「入学を皮切りに一人暮らしを始めた」→ ○「入学をきっかけに一人暮らしを始めた」.
The first item must itself be the first of that series and of the same kind as the rest: ○「東京公演を皮切りに、全国ツアーが始まる」 (the Tokyo show is also one stop on the tour).
It is fairly formal, used in news and business; for small everyday matters of your own it sounds grandiose, and 「〜から始めて」 will do.

daily.title: Following an idol
daily.description: Fans talk about their idol's tour schedule.
daily.example: I heard the Asia tour kicks off with the Osaka show next month.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report on a chain of events.
daily.example: Starting with one accusation, similar reports of harm followed one after another.

work.title: Business plan
work.description: A company announces its overseas expansion.
work.example: Starting with our Shanghai store, we will expand across Asia.

work.title: Event planning
work.description: Explaining the schedule of a series of events.
work.example: Starting with the April seminar, we will hold training sessions throughout the year.

etymology: 「皮切り」 originally meant the very first burn in moxibustion. That first burn on the skin hurts the most, so it was called “cutting the skin”. Later it came to mean “the very beginning” of something.

similar.title: 〜をきっかけに
similar.explanation: The easiest to confuse. 「をきっかけに」 only gives the trigger, and the second clause can be a single change or action; 「を皮切りに」 requires a series of similar events in the second clause, with the first clause as its opening item.

similar.title: 〜を契機に
similar.explanation: Same as 「をきっかけに」, meaning “taking ... as the turning point”, and the second clause is usually a major change; 「を皮切りに」 is not about turning points but about “starting from A, one after another”.

similar.title: 〜をはじめ
similar.explanation: Both put A at the head of a series of similar things. 「をはじめ」 names a representative (「東京をはじめ、大阪、名古屋でも」) without time order; 「を皮切りに」 stresses unfolding in time.

formation: Built from the noun 「皮切り」 + 「を」 + 「に（として）」. 「皮切り」 originally meant the first moxibustion burn (the most painful, as if cutting the skin) and extended to “the first of a series of things”. 「Aを皮切りに」 = “taking A as the first stroke”: if there is a “first”, a second and third are assumed to follow, so the second clause must be similar events continuing one after another. This is exactly the difference from 「をきっかけに」, which only names a trigger.

meaning: Written style. One cannot help feeling a certain emotion about something.
connection: Noun (同情, 怒り, 驚き, 涙, 憤り, etc.) + を禁じ得ない

senses.label: Cannot help feeling ...
senses.meaning: After seeing or hearing something, a strong emotion wells up naturally and can't be held back. It follows emotion nouns. Formal, used in writing or official statements.
senses.connection: Emotion noun + を禁じ得ない / を禁じ得なかった / を禁じ得ません
examples: Hearing the disaster victims' stories, I couldn't help feeling sympathy for them.
I can't help feeling angry at such an unfair ruling.
I cannot help being astonished at the truth behind that incident.

notes: Only emotion nouns can precede it (同情・怒り・驚き・涙・憤り・失笑), not verbs: ✕「泣くことを禁じ得ない」→ ○「涙を禁じ得ない」.
It normally expresses feelings that well up in the speaker facing an outside event; for a third person add something like 「ようだ」: 「彼も驚きを禁じ得ないようだった」.
「失笑を禁じ得ない」 means “can't help laughing”, with a contemptuous edge, and is very rude when applied to someone's remarks or work.
「禁じ得ない」 means “cannot suppress (one's own feeling)”, not “cannot forbid (others)”; do not read it the wrong way round literally.

daily.title: Reading the news
daily.description: Reading a report about an outrageous crime.
daily.example: I can't help feeling indignant at crimes that target the vulnerable.

daily.title: Watching a documentary
daily.description: Moved by a touching documentary.
daily.example: The way he lived his life brought me to tears.

work.title: Official statement
work.description: A company issues a statement about an accident.
work.example: We deeply regret this accident.

work.title: Book review
work.description: A critic reviews a work.
work.example: One cannot help but marvel at the depth of the author's insight.

etymology: 「禁じる」 means “to forbid, to suppress”, and 「得ない」 means “cannot”. Literally: “cannot suppress (this feeling)”.

similar.title: 〜ずにはいられない
similar.explanation: Close; both mean “can't help”. 「ずにはいられない」 follows verbs and means being unable to stop an action (「笑わずにはいられない」), and works in speech and writing; 「を禁じ得ない」 follows emotion nouns and is stiff written language.

similar.title: 〜てならない
similar.explanation: Both express strong feelings that are hard to restrain. 「てならない」 follows adjectives or verb te-forms (「残念でならない」) and mostly describes a lasting feeling; 「を禁じ得ない」 is mostly a feeling that wells up on the spot at some event.

similar.title: 〜に堪えない
similar.explanation: Close with emotion nouns (「感謝に堪えない」). 「に堪えない」 is mostly for formal speech expressing thanks or regret; 「を禁じ得ない」 is mostly for sympathy, anger or surprise.

similar.title: 〜得る・〜得ない
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「禁じ得ない」 is 「禁じる」 + 「得ない」 (“cannot”). 「得ない」 attaches to many verbs (「ありえない」, 「理解し得ない」); 「禁じ得ない」 is one fixed expression among them.

formation: Built from the continuative 「禁じ」 of 「禁じる」 (“to forbid, to suppress”) + 「得ない」 (the negative of 「得る」, “cannot”), literally “cannot suppress”. What precedes 「を」 is the thing being suppressed, namely the feeling rising in the heart, so only emotion nouns fit. The whole means “I try to hold this feeling down but cannot”, with nothing to do with forbidding others. This “Sino-Japanese verb + 得ない” structure has a kanbun-reading flavor, so it is solemn written language.

meaning: Written style. Marks means or method, “with, by means of ...”; also a time limit, “as of ... (ending)”.
connection: Noun + をもって / をもちまして (more polite)

senses.label: By means of ...
senses.meaning: The means, method or attitude used to do something. Like 「で」, but formal. Common in official notices and writing.
senses.connection: Noun (書面, 誠意, 拍手, etc.) + をもって. Common: 「書面をもって」, 「誠意をもって」, 「身をもって」
examples: We will notify you of the results in writing.
He apologized sincerely.
The athletes were welcomed with warm applause.

senses.label: As of ... (deadline)
senses.meaning: Something ends at this point in time. Used to formally announce an end or a deadline. The politer form is 「をもちまして」.
senses.connection: Time noun (本日, 今月末, 〇月〇日, etc.) + をもって / をもちまして + ending, closing, leaving, etc.
examples: We will be closing our business as of today.
I will be leaving the company as of March 31.
This concludes the meeting.

senses.label: As the standard
senses.meaning: Marks the standard or basis for a decision. Common in rules and regulations.
senses.connection: Noun + をもって + 〜とする
examples: A score of 60 or higher counts as a pass.
Confirmation of attendance will serve as registration.

notes: The time use marks a point, mostly an ending (「本日をもって閉店」 = today is the last day), but it can also mark a start (「四月一日をもって社長に就任」). Check the second clause before deciding, or you will mix up “end” and “start”.
The means use mostly takes abstract nouns (誠意・書面・実力・拍手), not everyday concrete tools: ✕「ペンをもって書く」→ ○「ペンで書く」.
When announcing an ending to customers or an audience, 「をもちまして」 is the proper form (「これをもちまして閉会いたします」); 「をもって」 sounds stiff in spoken addresses.
The 「持って」 in 「傘を持って」 means “holding” and is unrelated; in kanji this grammar is written 「以て」.

daily.title: Store announcement
daily.description: An announcement before a shopping mall closes.
daily.example: Today's business hours will end at 8 p.m.

daily.title: Sharing an experience
daily.description: Telling a friend about something you learned firsthand.
daily.example: I learned firsthand how important health is.

work.title: Official notice
work.description: HR informs applicants of the results.
work.example: We will inform you in writing at a later date whether you have been hired.

work.title: Chairing a meeting
work.description: The chair announces the end of the meeting.
work.example: With that, we will conclude today's meeting.

work.title: Farewell email
work.description: An employee sends a goodbye email to everyone.
work.example: I will be leaving the company at the end of September.

etymology: 「もって」 is a sound-changed form of 「持ちて」. In kanbun reading it was used to read the character 「以」, so it took on the meaning “by means of”. It is often written 「以て」.

similar.title: 〜で (means / method)
similar.explanation: The everyday way to say means or method. 「で」 works in speech and writing and takes concrete tools (「ペンで書く」); 「をもって」 is only for formal occasions and mostly takes abstract nouns.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: Both can express means (「話し合いによって解決する」). 「によって」 is more neutral and has wider uses; 「をもって」 is more formal, often seen in notices, commendations and speeches.

similar.title: 〜を限りに
similar.explanation: Close in the deadline sense. 「をもって」 just marks the point in time and can also mark a start; 「を限りに」 only means “this is the last, never again after this”, with a tone of farewell.

similar.title: 〜をもってすれば／〜をもってしても
similar.explanation: Same origin: add 「すれば／しても」 to the means use of 「をもって」 to get “with A alone, ... can be done / even with A, ... cannot be done”, used to evaluate how powerful A is.

formation: 「もって」 is the 「持って」 that came from the sound change of 「持ちて」, from the verb 「持つ」. In kanbun reading it was used to read the character 「以」 (「以A為B」), so 「Aをもって」 is “taking A, by means of A” → means or method. Treating a time noun as “the point taken to draw a line”, 「本日をもって」 = “with today as the cutoff” → a deadline. 「AをもってBとする」 reads the kanbun 「以A為B」 directly → a standard or a ruling. All three senses come from kanbun 「以」, so the whole is stiff written language, written 「以て」 in kanji.
